claim: SMG1 is a PI3K-related kinase (PIKK) that monitors the progression of metazoan nonsense-mediated mRNA decay (NMD) by phosphorylating the RNA helicase UPF1.
source: The PI3K-related kinase (PIKK) SMG1 monitors the progression of metazoan nonsense-mediated mRNA decay (NMD) by phosphorylating the RNA helicase UPF1.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and is supported by citations in the introduction.

claim: The activity of SMG1 is impaired by small molecule inhibitors.
source: Previous work has shown that the activity of SMG1 is impaired by small molecule inhibitors, is reduced by the SMG1 interactors SMG8 and SMG9, and is downregulated by the so-called SMG1 insertion domain.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as previous work, implying citation-based evidence.

claim: The activity of SMG1 is reduced by the SMG1 interactors SMG8 and SMG9.
source: Previous work has shown that the activity of SMG1 is impaired by small molecule inhibitors, is reduced by the SMG1 interactors SMG8 and SMG9, and is downregulated by the so-called SMG1 insertion domain.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as previous work, implying citation-based evidence.

claim: The activity of SMG1 is downregulated by the SMG1 insertion domain.
source: Previous work has shown that the activity of SMG1 is impaired by small molecule inhibitors, is reduced by the SMG1 interactors SMG8 and SMG9, and is downregulated by the so-called SMG1 insertion domain.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as previous work, implying citation-based evidence.

claim: Cryo-electron microscopy reconstructions of human SMG1-9 and SMG1-8-9 complexes bound to either a SMG1 inhibitor or a non-hydrolyzable ATP analog were obtained at overall resolutions ranging from 2.8 to 3.6 Å.
source: Here, we present cryo-electron microscopy reconstructions of human SMG1-9 and SMG1-8-9 complexes bound to either a SMG1 inhibitor or a non-hydrolyzable ATP analog at overall resolutions ranging from 2.8 to 3.6 Å.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the experimental results obtained in this study.

claim: The structures reveal the basis with which a small molecule inhibitor preferentially targets SMG1 over other PIKKs.
source: These structures reveal the basis with which a small molecule inhibitor preferentially targets SMG1 over other PIKKs.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a finding from the structural data.

claim: The SMG1 insertion domain can exert an autoinhibitory function by directly blocking the substrate-binding path as well as overall access to the SMG1 kinase active site.
source: By comparison with our previously reported substrate-bound structure (Langer et al.,2020), we show that the SMG1 insertion domain can exert an autoinhibitory function by directly blocking the substrate-binding path as well as overall access to the SMG1 kinase active site.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by structural comparison with previous work.

claim: SMG1 autoinhibition is stabilized by the presence of SMG8.
source: Together with biochemical analysis, our data indicate that SMG1 autoinhibition is stabilized by the presence of SMG8.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a conclusion from both structural and biochemical data.

claim: Translation termination at a premature stop codon triggers phosphorylation of the RNA helicase UPF1.
source: In metazoans, translation termination at a premature stop codon triggers phosphorylation of the RNA helicase UPF1, which then enables the recruitment of downstream effectors, in turn resulting in the degradation of the targeted mRNA by ribonucleases (Ohnishi et al., 2003; Yamashita, 2013; Chakrabarti et al., 2014; Nicholson et al., 2014; Okada-Katsuhata et al., 2012; Kashima et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with multiple supporting citations.

claim: UPF1 phosphorylation enables the recruitment of downstream effectors, resulting in the degradation of the targeted mRNA by ribonucleases.
source: In metazoans, translation termination at a premature stop codon triggers phosphorylation of the RNA helicase UPF1, which then enables the recruitment of downstream effectors, in turn resulting in the degradation of the targeted mRNA by ribonucleases (Ohnishi et al., 2003; Yamashita, 2013; Chakrabarti et al., 2014; Nicholson et al., 2014; Okada-Katsuhata et al., 2012; Kashima et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with multiple supporting citations.

claim: UPF1 phosphorylation is a crucial point in metazoan NMD.
source: UPF1 phosphorylation is thus a crucial point in metazoan NMD; it occurs specifically at particular Ser-containing motifs and is mediated by the SMG1 kinase (Denning et al., 2001; Yamashita et al., 2001).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: UPF1 phosphorylation occurs specifically at particular Ser-containing motifs and is mediated by the SMG1 kinase.
source: UPF1 phosphorylation is thus a crucial point in metazoan NMD; it occurs specifically at particular Ser-containing motifs and is mediated by the SMG1 kinase (Denning et al., 2001; Yamashita et al., 2001).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: SMG1 is a member of the phosphatidylinositol-3-kinase-related kinase (PIKK) family.
source: SMG1 is a member of the phosphatidylinositol-3-kinase-related kinase (PIKK) family, which also includes the ATM, ATR, DNA-PKc, and mTOR kinases (Keith and Schreiber, 1995).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: The PIKK family includes the ATM, ATR, DNA-PKc, and mTOR kinases.
source: SMG1 is a member of the phosphatidylinositol-3-kinase-related kinase (PIKK) family, which also includes the ATM, ATR, DNA-PKc, and mTOR kinases (Keith and Schreiber, 1995).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: All active PIKKs are Ser-Thr protein kinases.
source: Despite the confounding name reflecting a possible evolutionary origin with a lipid kinase (Keith and Schreiber, 1995), and in retrospect the ability of some PIKK family members to bind inositol-6-phosphate (Gat et al., 2019), all active PIKKs are Ser-Thr protein kinases.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Some PIKK family members can bind inositol-6-phosphate.
source: Despite the confounding name reflecting a possible evolutionary origin with a lipid kinase (Keith and Schreiber, 1995), and in retrospect the ability of some PIKK family members to bind inositol-6-phosphate (Gat et al., 2019), all active PIKKs are Ser-Thr protein kinases.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: PIKKs share an overall similar architecture comprising a C-terminal catalytic module (FAT, kinase, and FATC domains) and an N-terminal α-solenoid.
source: These large, multidomain enzymes share an overall similar architecture: a C-terminal catalytic module (comprising the so-called FAT, kinase, and FATC domains) and an N-terminal α-solenoid (that typically serves as a protein-protein interaction module).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as established knowledge about PIKKs.

claim: The N-terminal α-solenoid of PIKKs typically serves as a protein-protein interaction module.
source: These large, multidomain enzymes share an overall similar architecture: a C-terminal catalytic module (comprising the so-called FAT, kinase, and FATC domains) and an N-terminal α-solenoid (that typically serves as a protein-protein interaction module).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as established knowledge about PIKKs.

claim: PIKKs bind to and are regulated by interacting proteins, with which they form large and dynamic assemblies.
source: Indeed, PIKKs bind to and are regulated by interacting proteins, with which they form large and dynamic assemblies.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as established knowledge about PIKKs.

claim: Some PIKKs contain an autoregulatory element known as the PIKK-regulatory domain (PRD) in the variable region connecting the kinase and FATC domains.
source: In addition, some PIKKs contain an autoregulatory element, particularly in the variable region connecting the kinase and FATC domains, that is known as the PIKK-regulatory domain (PRD) (Baretić and Williams, 2014; Imseng et al., 2018; Jansma and Hopfner, 2021).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: The kinase domains of PIKKs have been the target of numerous efforts in the development of specific inhibitors.
source: Finally, the kinase domains of PIKKs have been the target of numerous efforts in the development of specific inhibitors.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as established knowledge.

claim: Small molecules targeting specific PIKKs have been approved as therapeutics or are being evaluated in clinical trials.
source: Not surprisingly, given the central roles of these kinases in pathways surveilling cellular homeostasis, small molecules targeting specific PIKKs have been approved as therapeutics or are being evaluated in clinical trials (Janku et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2011; Durant et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: The high conservation of the PIKK kinase domain has complicated efforts to develop inhibitors specifically targeting only a selected member of this family of enzymes.
source: Nevertheless, the high conservation of the PIKK kinase domain has complicated efforts to develop inhibitors specifically targeting only a selected member of this family of enzymes.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as established knowledge.

claim: Structural data rationalizing the binding specificity of PIKK inhibitors are still sparse in general and entirely missing for the SMG1 kinase.
source: Structural data rationalizing the binding specificity of such compounds to PIKKs are still sparse in general and entirely missing for the SMG1 kinase.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a gap in knowledge.

claim: SMG8 and SMG9 have been linked to dysregulated NMD and neurodevelopmental disorders in humans.
source: In the case of SMG1, the two interacting factors SMG8 and SMG9 have been linked to dysregulated NMD and neurodevelopmental disorders in humans (Alzahrani et al., 2020; Shaheen et al., 2016; Yamashita et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: SMG8 and SMG9 form an unusual G-domain heterodimer.
source: SMG8 and SMG9 form an unusual G-domain heterodimer (Gat et al., 2019; Langer et al., 2020; Li et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: The G-domain of SMG9 binds both the α-solenoid and the catalytic module of SMG1.
source: The G-domain of SMG9 binds both the α-solenoid and the catalytic module of SMG1 while the G-domain of SMG8 engages only the α-solenoid, thus rationalizing biochemical studies pointing to the crucial role of SMG9 in enabling the incorporation of SMG8 into the complex (Yamashita et al., 2009; Arias-Palomo et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: The G-domain of SMG8 engages only the α-solenoid of SMG1.
source: The G-domain of SMG9 binds both the α-solenoid and the catalytic module of SMG1 while the G-domain of SMG8 engages only the α-solenoid, thus rationalizing biochemical studies pointing to the crucial role of SMG9 in enabling the incorporation of SMG8 into the complex (Yamashita et al., 2009; Arias-Palomo et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: SMG9 plays a crucial role in enabling the incorporation of SMG8 into the SMG1 complex.
source: The G-domain of SMG9 binds both the α-solenoid and the catalytic module of SMG1 while the G-domain of SMG8 engages only the α-solenoid, thus rationalizing biochemical studies pointing to the crucial role of SMG9 in enabling the incorporation of SMG8 into the complex (Yamashita et al., 2009; Arias-Palomo et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Removal or C-terminal truncation of SMG8 results in hyper-activation of SMG1 kinase activity.
source: In turn, SMG8 appears to have a direct regulatory function on SMG1, as its removal or C-terminal truncation results in hyper-activation of SMG1 kinase activity (Yamashita et al., 2009; Deniaud et al., 2015; Arias-Palomo et al., 2011; Zhu et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: The C-terminal domain of SMG8 remains poorly defined in all available cryo-EM reconstructions.
source: However, the C-terminal domain of SMG8 remains poorly defined in all available cryo-EM reconstructions (Zhu et al., 2019; Gat et al., 2019; Langer et al., 2020), hindering a molecular understanding of its regulatory role.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Removal of the SMG1 insertion domain causes hyper-activation of the kinase.
source: Removal of the SMG1 insertion domain causes hyper-activation of the kinase (Deniaud et al., 2015; Zhu et al., 2019), similarly to the effect reported for the PRDs of other PIKKs (McMahon et al., 2002; Edinger and Thompson, 2004; Xiao et al., 2019; Mordes et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: The SMG1 insertion domain shows no sequence similarity to the PRDs of other PIKKs and is remarkably larger in comparison.
source: However, the SMG1 insertion domain shows no sequence similarity to the PRDs of other PIKKs and is remarkably larger in comparison.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as an observation about sequence analysis.

claim: None of the current cryo-EM reconstructions of SMG1 or its complexes show density corresponding to the SMG1 insertion domain.
source: None of the current cryo-EM reconstructions of SMG1 or its complexes show density corresponding to the SMG1 insertion domain (Zhu et al., 2019; Gat et al., 2019; Langer et al., 2020), and it is thus unclear how it regulates kinase activity.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: SMG1i is a small-molecule compound based on a pyrimidine derivative that has been reported to inhibit SMG1 catalytic activity.
source: We set out to study the inhibitory mechanism of SMG1i (Figure 1A), a small-molecule compound based on a pyrimidine derivative that has been reported to inhibit SMG1 catalytic activity (Gopalsamy et al., 2012; Mino et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with supporting citations.

claim: A significant reduction of UPF1-LSQ phosphorylation was observed when adding SMG1i at concentrations equimolar to the enzyme.
source: In this assay, we observed a significant reduction of UPF1-LSQ phosphorylation when adding SMG1i at concentrations equimolar to the enzyme (Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: A reduction in UPF1 phosphorylation was observed in the presence of low micromolar amounts of SMG1i using a radioactivity-based phosphorylation assay.
source: Again, we observed a reduction in UPF1 phosphorylation in the presence of low micromolar amounts of SMG1i (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: SMG1i only affected mTOR activity in the highest concentration range, well beyond concentrations that had an observable effect on SMG1 activity.
source: We observed that SMG1i only affected mTOR activity in the highest concentration range, well beyond concentrations that had an observable effect on SMG1 activity (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.

claim: SMG1i robustly inhibited SMG1 while mTOR activity was only weakly affected.
source: Upon quantifying the levels of phosphorylation using densitometry and normalizing them to the amount of protein loaded in each lane, we found that SMG1i robustly inhibited SMG1 while mTOR activity was only weakly affected (Figure 1F, Figure 1—figure supplement 2D, E,F).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: SMG1i displays high potency and specificity in inhibiting the SMG1 kinase in vitro.
source: In agreement with previous results (Gopalsamy et al., 2012), we concluded that SMG1i displays high potency and specificity in inhibiting the SMG1 kinase in vitro.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a conclusion from the experimental data and previous work.

claim: The cryo-EM reconstruction of SMG1-8-9 bound to SMG1i reached an overall resolution of 3.1 Å.
source: The resulting reconstruction reached an overall resolution of 3.1 Å, and we observed clear density for the SMG1 inhibitor bound to the kinase active site (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplements 1 and 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 3B, C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by the figures.

claim: Clear density for the SMG1 inhibitor bound to the kinase active site was observed in the cryo-EM reconstruction.
source: The resulting reconstruction reached an overall resolution of 3.1 Å, and we observed clear density for the SMG1 inhibitor bound to the kinase active site (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplements 1 and 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 3B, C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by the figures.

claim: SMG1i exploits essentially the same binding site as the ATP analog AMPPNP.
source: Superposition with our previously published AMPPNP- and substrate-bound model (Langer et al., 2020) revealed that SMG1i exploits essentially the same binding site as the ATP analog.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on structural comparison.

claim: SMG1i wedges deeper in between the N- and C-lobe of the kinase domain and is engaged in more extensive interactions than AMPPNP.
source: However, SMG1i wedges deeper in between the N- and C-lobe of the kinase domain and is engaged in more extensive interactions (Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 3A and D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by the figures.

claim: SMG1i is a potent ATP-competitive inhibitor.
source: These observations identify SMG1i as a potent ATP-competitive inhibitor.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a conclusion from the structural data.

claim: SMG1 Pro2213 and Asp2339 contact the sulfonamide moiety of SMG1i.
source: While many of the SMG1 residues interacting with SMG1i are conserved within the PIKK family, two contact sites appear to be specific: SMG1 Pro2213 and Asp2339 contact the sulfonamide moiety of the inhibitor while Asn2356 forms hydrogen bonds with the phenyl urea/carbamide group (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 2B.

claim: SMG1 Asn2356 forms hydrogen bonds with the phenyl urea/carbamide group of SMG1i.
source: While many of the SMG1 residues interacting with SMG1i are conserved within the PIKK family, two contact sites appear to be specific: SMG1 Pro2213 and Asp2339 contact the sulfonamide moiety of the inhibitor while Asn2356 forms hydrogen bonds with the phenyl urea/carbamide group (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 2B.

claim: The corresponding residues in mTOR (Thr2245 and Ser2342) would not be able to mediate analogous interactions with the SMG1i sulfonamide group.
source: Superposition of the SMG1 active site in the SMG1i-bound structure with the active site of mTORΔN shows that the corresponding residues have diverged and would not be able to mediate analogous interactions with the SMG1i sulfonamide group (mTOR Thr2245 and Ser2342 at the positions of SMG1 Pro2213 and Asp2339) or with the urea group (mTOR Gly2359 at the position of SMG1 Asn2356) (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 2C.

claim: mTOR Gly2359 at the position of SMG1 Asn2356 would not be able to mediate analogous interactions with the SMG1i urea group.
source: Superposition of the SMG1 active site in the SMG1i-bound structure with the active site of mTORΔN shows that the corresponding residues have diverged and would not be able to mediate analogous interactions with the SMG1i sulfonamide group (mTOR Thr2245 and Ser2342 at the positions of SMG1 Pro2213 and Asp2339) or with the urea group (mTOR Gly2359 at the position of SMG1 Asn2356) (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 2C.

claim: Subtle differences in the SMG1 structure underpin the specificity of the SMG1i inhibitor.
source: We conclude that subtle differences in the SMG1 structure underpin the specificity of the SMG1i inhibitor.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a conclusion from the structural comparisons.

claim: Additional density was observed near the end of the kinase domain in the reconstruction of the SMG1i-bound SMG1-8-9 complex, protruding from the position where the insertion domain is expected to start.
source: In the reconstruction of the SMG1i-bound SMG1-8-9 complex, we observed additional density near the end of the kinase domain, protruding from the position where the insertion domain is expected to start (Figure 3, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by the figures.

claim: The additional density observed in the SMG1i-bound SMG1-8-9 complex docks at the substrate-binding site of the kinase domain.
source: While the lower resolution for this part of the map was not sufficient to unambiguously build an atomic model, this density clearly docks at the substrate-binding site of the kinase domain (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A, B and C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by the figures.

claim: The additional density in the SMG1i-bound SMG1-8-9 reconstruction is mutually exclusive with the position of a bound substrate.
source: Superposition with the previous cryo-EM structure of SMG1-8-9 complex bound to a UPF1 peptide (Langer et al., 2020) revealed that the additional density in the current reconstruction is mutually exclusive with the position of a bound substrate (Figure 3I, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by the figures.

claim: The SMG1 insertion domain contains a PRD that can directly occupy and block the substrate-binding path in the kinase active site.
source: We concluded that the SMG1 insertion domain contains a PRD that can directly occupy and block the substrate-binding path in the kinase active site, analogous to other PIKKs.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a conclusion from the structural data.

claim: The SMG1 PRD would have to re-arrange upon substrate binding, as observed in the case of the inactive-to-active transition of DNA-PK.
source: The SMG1 PRD would have to re-arrange upon substrate binding, as observed in the case of the inactive-to-active transition of DNA-PK (Chen et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with a supporting citation.

claim: A subset of particles missing any density for SMG8 was isolated from the cryo-EM data set, representing an SMG1i-bound SMG1-9 complex.
source: Within the cryo-EM data set collected on an SMG1-8-9 complex incubated with SMG1i, we isolated a subset of particles missing any density for SMG8, hence representing an SMG1i-bound SMG1-9 complex (Figure 3B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1C, Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by the figures.

claim: The reconstruction of SMG1i-bound SMG1-9 complex reached 3.6 Å resolution.
source: The corresponding 3.6 Å reconstruction not only showed a similar mode of interaction of SMG1i, but also several features distinct from SMG1 in isolation and the SMG1-8-9 ternary complex.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section.

claim: The α-solenoid of SMG1 rearranges upon binding first SMG9 and then SMG8, consistent with a stepwise compaction of SMG1.
source: Globally, the α-solenoid of SMG1 rearranges, consistent with the notion of a stepwise compaction of SMG1 upon binding first SMG9 and then SMG8 (Figure 3—figure supplement 4A and B; Melero et al., 2014; Zhu et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by the figures and citations.

claim: The reconstruction of SMG1-9 showed no ordered density at the active site for the PRD.
source: Importantly, the reconstruction of SMG1-9 showed no ordered density at the active site for the PRD (Figure 3B and II, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A), which is in contrast to the ordered PRD density visualized in the SMG1i-bound SMG1-8-9 complex.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by the figures.

claim: Maps for SMG1-8-9 and SMG1-9 bound to AMPPNP were obtained at overall resolutions of 2.8 Å and 3.1 Å, respectively.
source: We obtained maps for SMG1-8-9 and SMG1-9 at overall resolutions of 2.8 Å and 3.1 Å, respectively (Figure 3C and D, Figure 3—figure supplements 2 and 3).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by the figures.

claim: Both reconstructions of AMPPNP-bound complexes showed clear density for AMPPNP in the SMG1 active site.
source: Both reconstructions showed clear density for AMPPNP in the SMG1 active site.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section.

claim: In the reconstruction of the ternary SMG1-8-9 complex with AMPPNP, additional density was observed at the substrate-binding site, in the same position as that observed when in the presence of SMG1i.
source: In the reconstruction of the ternary SMG1-8-9 complex, we observed an additional density at the substrate-binding site, in the same position as that observed when in the presence of SMG1i (Figure 3III, IV).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by the figures.

claim: The SMG1 inhibitor has a stabilizing effect on the autoinhibitory conformation of the SMG1 PRD.
source: It thus appears that the SMG1 inhibitor has a stabilizing effect on the autoinhibitory conformation of the SMG1 PRD.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an inference from the structural data.

claim: In the reconstruction of the binary SMG1-9 complex in the presence of AMPPNP, no ordered density was observed at the substrate-binding site.
source: In the reconstruction of the binary SMG1-9 complex in the presence of AMPPNP, we observed no ordered density at the substrate-binding site, consistent with the reconstruction obtained in the presence of SMG1i.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section.

claim: The autoinhibitory conformation of the PRD in the insertion domain of SMG1 is connected to the presence of a nucleotide in the ATP-binding site and is stabilized by the presence of SMG8.
source: We concluded that the autoinhibitory conformation of the PRD in the insertion domain of SMG1 is connected to the presence of a nucleotide in the ATP-binding site and is stabilized by the presence of SMG8.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a conclusion from the structural data.

claim: Improved density for the C-terminal domain of SMG8 was achieved by further processing of the SMG1i-bound SMG1-8-9 data, showing a knob-like feature directly connected to the end of the stalk and in turn connecting to a larger globular mass.
source: By further processing of the SMG1i-bound SMG1-8-9 data, we could achieve improved density for the C-terminal domain of SMG8, showing a knob-like feature directly connected to the end of the stalk and in turn connecting to a larger globular mass (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 4A.

claim: Additional density extending from the location of the PRD wraps along the catalytic module of SMG1, occludes the access to the kinase active site, and reaches toward the IP6-binding site.
source: Concurrently, we observed an additional density extending from the location of the PRD that we attributed to the SMG1 insertion domain (see below). On one side, this density wraps along the catalytic module of SMG1, occludes the access to the kinase active site (Figure 4A), and reaches toward the IP6-binding site (Figure 4A and C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 4A and C.

claim: The density attributed to the SMG1 insertion domain projects into solvent and approaches the globular SMG8 C-terminal region.
source: On the other side, the density projects into solvent and approaches the globular SMG8 C-terminal region.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section.

claim: The close proximity of the SMG1 insertion domain and the SMG8 C-terminal domain suggested a physical contact between these two parts of the SMG1-8-9 complex.
source: Although the low resolution of this part of the map did not allow model building, the close proximity suggested a physical contact between the SMG1 insertion domain and the SMG8 C-terminal domain.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an inference from the structural data.

claim: Reproducible intra cross-links were observed between the end of the SMG1 insertion and the catalytic module, in particular the FAT and kinase domains.
source: We also observed reproducible intra cross-links between the end of the SMG1 insertion and the catalytic module, in particular the FAT (residues 823–1938) and kinase (residues 2080–2422) domains (Figure 4B and C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 4B and C.

claim: Inter cross-links were detected between the SMG1 insertion domain and the SMG8 C-terminal domain.
source: Importantly, we detected inter cross-links between the SMG1 insertion domain and the SMG8 C-terminal domain (Figure 4B), consistent with the proximity of the EM densities (Figure 4A) and previously reported XL-MS data (Deniaud et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 4B and previous work.

claim: The SMG1 insertion domain co-precipitated the SMG8 C-terminus in low-salt conditions.
source: We observed that the SMG1 insertion domain indeed co-precipitated the SMG8 C-terminus in these conditions (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 4D.

claim: Increasing the salt concentration had a detrimental effect on the SMG8 C-terminus—SMG1 insertion co-precipitation.
source: As anticipated, increasing the salt concentration had a detrimental effect on the SMG8 C-terminus—SMG1 insertion co-precipitation (Figure 4—figure supplement 4A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 4—figure supplement 4A.

claim: There exists a direct physical link between the SMG1 insertion domain and SMG8 C-terminus.
source: Taken together, these experiments indicate the existence not just of proximity but of a direct physical link between the SMG1 insertion domain and SMG8 C-terminus, rationalizing the observed dependency of SMG1 autoinhibition on the presence of SMG8 (Figure 3).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a conclusion from the experiments.

claim: SMG1i binds to the ATP-binding site within the kinase active site.
source: In this manuscript, we reported a reconstruction of the SMG1-8-9 complex bound to an SMG1 inhibitor. We showed that this compound binds to the ATP-binding site within the kinase active site.
evidence: This is stated in the Conclusions section.

claim: Two functional groups within SMG1i possibly confer specificity to SMG1 over related kinases.
source: By comparison with structural data of related kinases, we identified two functional groups within the small molecule that possibly confer specificity to SMG1.
evidence: This is stated in the Conclusions section.

claim: The N-terminal part of the SMG1 insertion domain acts as a PRD and occupied the substrate-binding path within the SMG1 active site.
source: In addition to the SMG1 inhibitor, we observed density for the N-terminal part of the SMG1 insertion domain in the SMG1-8-9 reconstruction. This part of the insertion domain acts as a PRD and occupied the substrate-binding path within the SMG1 active site.
evidence: This is stated in the Conclusions section.

claim: A PRD within the SMG1 insertion domain can restrict access to the kinase active site, consistent with data for other PIKKs.
source: Consistent with data for other PIKKs, a PRD within the SMG1 insertion domain can therefore restrict access to the kinase active site.
evidence: This is stated in the Conclusions section.

claim: An interaction between the SMG1 insertion and SMG8 is important for stabilizing the autoinhibited state of the complex.
source: The structure of an SMG1i-bound SMG1-9 complex reconstructed from the same data set as SMG1i-bound SMG1-8-9 did not show ordered density for the SMG1 PRD in the SMG1 active site. This suggested that an interaction between the SMG1 insertion and SMG8 was important for stabilizing the autoinhibited state of the complex.
evidence: This is stated in the Conclusions section.

claim: Biochemical analysis indicated a direct physical link between parts of the SMG1 insertion domain and the C-terminal domain of SMG8.
source: Consistently, our biochemical analysis indicated a direct physical link between parts of the SMG1 insertion domain and the C-terminal domain of SMG8.
evidence: This is stated in the Conclusions section.

claim: Blockage of the substrate-binding path is also possible when the SMG1-8-9 complex active site is bound to a nucleotide.
source: While autoinhibition was not observed in previously published apo-structures, our reconstructions of SMG1-9 and SMG1-8-9 bound to AMPPNP showed that blockage of the substrate-binding path was also possible when the SMG1-8-9 complex active site was bound to a nucleotide.
evidence: This is stated in the Conclusions section.

claim: The described autoinhibition is not a phenomenon limited to the inhibitor-bound structures.
source: Accordingly, the described autoinhibition was not a phenomenon limited to the inhibitor-bound structures.
evidence: This is stated in the Conclusions section.

claim: At least two layers of regulation of SMG1 kinase activity exist: access to the SMG1 active site can be restricted in cis by a PRD within the SMG1 insertion domain, and this autoinhibition is stabilized in trans by the SMG8 C-terminus.
source: We conclude that at least two layers of regulation of SMG1 kinase activity exist: first, access to the SMG1 active site can be restricted in cis by a PRD within the SMG1 insertion domain. Second, this autoinhibition is stabilized in trans by the SMG8 C-terminus.
evidence: This is stated in the Conclusions section as a summary of the findings.

claim: The efficiency of UPF1 co-precipitation was unaffected by the presence of SMG1i.
source: The efficiency of UPF1 co-precipitation was unaffected by the presence of SMG1i, suggesting that either UPF1 can overcome blockage of the SMG1 active site by the SMG1 insertion domain or has secondary binding sites independent of the observed SMG1 autoinhibition.
evidence: This is stated in the Conclusions section and supported by experimental data.

claim: UPF1 can overcome blockage of the SMG1 active site by the SMG1 insertion domain or has secondary binding sites independent of the observed SMG1 autoinhibition.
source: The efficiency of UPF1 co-precipitation was unaffected by the presence of SMG1i, suggesting that either UPF1 can overcome blockage of the SMG1 active site by the SMG1 insertion domain or has secondary binding sites independent of the observed SMG1 autoinhibition.
evidence: This is stated in the Conclusions section as a speculation based on experimental data.

claim: UPF1-binding and SMG1 autoinhibition might be able to occur in parallel.
source: Indeed, superposition of the autoinhibited complex reconstruction with a previously reported negative-stain map of a cross-linked UPF1-bound SMG1-8-9 complex raised the possibility that UPF1-binding and SMG1 autoinhibition might be able to occur in parallel (Figure 4—figure supplement 4C).
evidence: This is stated in the Conclusions section and supported by Figure 4—figure supplement 4C.

claim: Optimal positioning of UPF1 with respect to the SMG1 kinase will allow the unstructured N- and C-terminal ends of UPF1 to efficiently compete with the SMG1 insertion domain for binding to the SMG1 active site in vivo.
source: An alternative explanation would be that optimal positioning of UPF1 with respect to the SMG1 kinase will allow the unstructured N- and C-terminal ends of UPF1 to efficiently compete with the SMG1 insertion domain for binding to the SMG1 active site in vivo.
evidence: This is stated in the Conclusions section as a speculation.

claim: SMG8 plays a crucial role in recruiting SMG1 complex to the NMD-competent messenger ribonucleoprotein particle.
source: Early biochemical experiments have suggested that SMG8 plays a crucial role in recruiting SMG1 complex to the NMD-competent messenger ribonucleoprotein particle (Yamashita et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the Conclusions section with a supporting citation.

claim: The SMG1-8-9 complex actively phosphorylated UPF1 in in vitro experiments using purified proteins.
source: Given that the SMG1-8-9 complex actively phosphorylated UPF1 in in vitro experiments using purified proteins and our observation that SMG1i binding did not impair the interaction of SMG1 with UPF1, it is tempting to speculate that UPF1 itself might be sufficient to overcome the effect of SMG8 on stabilizing SMG1 autoinhibition within an SMG1-8-9 complex.
evidence: This is stated in the Conclusions section as an observation from experiments.

claim: UPF1 itself might be sufficient to overcome the effect of SMG8 on stabilizing SMG1 autoinhibition within an SMG1-8-9 complex.
source: Given that the SMG1-8-9 complex actively phosphorylated UPF1 in in vitro experiments using purified proteins and our observation that SMG1i binding did not impair the interaction of SMG1 with UPF1, it is tempting to speculate that UPF1 itself might be sufficient to overcome the effect of SMG8 on stabilizing SMG1 autoinhibition within an SMG1-8-9 complex.
evidence: This is stated in the Conclusions section as a speculation.

claim: Nucleotide binding and kinase activation could occur in two distinct steps during NMD: upon ATP binding, the kinase complex would adopt an autoinhibited conformation and only be licensed for specific phosphorylation of its target by the substrate itself.
source: In this model, nucleotide binding and kinase activation could occur in two distinct steps during NMD: upon ATP binding, the kinase complex would adopt an autoinhibited conformation and only be licensed for specific phosphorylation of its target by the substrate itself (Figure 5).
evidence: This is stated in the Conclusions section as a speculative model and supported by Figure 5.

claim: Autophosphorylation of the kinase complex may play a crucial role in kinase activation.
source: In addition, autophosphorylation of the kinase complex may play a crucial role in kinase activation.
evidence: This is stated in the Conclusions section as a speculation.

claim: The structures will help to improve the design of selective PIKK active site inhibitors, for example, specific for SMG1.
source: Taken together, our structures will help to improve the design of selective PIKK active site inhibitors, for example, specific for SMG1.
evidence: This is stated in the Conclusions section as an implication of the work.

claim: The data suggest a unifying structural model for concerted action of the SMG1 insertion domain in cis and SMG8 in trans to tune SMG1 kinase activity.
source: Our data suggest a unifying structural model for concerted action of the SMG1 insertion domain in cis and SMG8 in trans to tune SMG1 kinase activity, shedding light on the intricate regulation of this kinase complex in metazoan NMD.
evidence: This is stated in the Conclusions section as a summary of the findings.
